questions.prompt: What is "environment strategy," as this course defines it?
options: The architectural decision of how many Salesforce environments to maintain, what each is for, and how work promotes between them safely
A Salesforce product purchased and installed from the AppExchange
A setting in Setup that automatically creates sandboxes on a schedule
The specific Apex design pattern used inside triggers
A once-a-year audit of production user licenses
A report type available only in Unlimited Edition
questions.explain: Environment strategy is a design decision architects make and justify -- how many environments exist, what each is for, and how changes move safely between them.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a purchasable product, not a strategy -- environment strategy is a design decision an architect makes, not something installed from the AppExchange. No single product substitutes for actually planning the environment hierarchy.

questions.prompt: A batch Apex job recalculating commissions passes every test against a 10,000-record sample in a Partial Copy testing sandbox, but fails to finish within governor limits against a Full sandbox's real 4-million-record table during staging. What does this most directly demonstrate?
options: Why staging, which uses data matching production's real volume, can catch problems a sampled testing environment cannot
That Partial Copy sandboxes are incapable of running any Apex code
That the bug should be patched directly inside the staging sandbox to avoid delaying the release
That governor limits only apply inside Full sandboxes, never in production
questions.explain: This is exactly the scenario staging exists for -- a sampled environment can hide a problem that only appears at real production data volume, which is why staging uses a Full sandbox rather than a Partial Copy.

questions.prompt: Match each sandbox type to what it carries and its typical use.
right: Metadata only, 1 GB storage, larger in-progress development projects
Metadata only, 200 MB storage, day-to-day building and unit testing
Matches production's full data and storage; staging and performance testing
A sampled subset of real records via a template, up to 5 GB; realistic QA and training
questions.explain: Developer and Developer Pro are both metadata-only, differing mainly in storage (200 MB vs. 1 GB). Partial Copy samples real data via a template; Full matches production completely and is the usual choice for staging.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Salesforce scratch org has a default lifespan of 7 days and a maximum allowed lifespan of ________ days, after which it expires permanently and cannot be restored.
questions.explain: A scratch org's duration is chosen at creation, from 1 to 30 days, with a default of 7 and a hard maximum of 30 -- expiration is permanent and by design.

questions.prompt: A team wants to move from long-lived Developer sandboxes, whose configuration was never fully captured anywhere else, to a scratch-org-based development approach. What risk does this course say they must address first?
options: None -- scratch orgs automatically import all existing sandbox configuration on creation
If the existing configuration was never fully committed to version control, a scratch org built purely from source will be missing whatever wasn't captured
Scratch orgs cannot be used by any team that has previously used a sandbox
Moving to scratch orgs first requires deleting every existing sandbox in the org
questions.explain: A scratch org only contains what source actually provides -- if a sandbox's accumulated configuration was never committed to version control, that gap surfaces as missing functionality once the team switches to scratch orgs.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about testing-tier practice, per this course.
options: Independent testing by someone other than the builder catches gaps a builder's own testing structurally cannot
Integration testing checks that interdependent pieces, like a Flow calling an Apex action, still work once combined
A change that fails testing should be promoted to staging anyway so staging can confirm the failure
Partial Copy sandboxes are the usual fit for integration testing and UAT because they offer realistic data without a Full sandbox's full cost
Unit testing and integration testing are two names for the exact same kind of check
questions.explain: Independent testing and integration testing are both accurately described, and Partial Copy's realistic-sample fit for this tier is correct. A failed test should go back to Development, not forward to staging, and unit testing (a single piece in isolation) is distinct from integration testing (pieces combined).

questions.prompt: Why does this course say a Full sandbox is the standard choice for staging rather than a Partial Copy sandbox?
options: Because Full sandboxes refresh faster than Partial Copy sandboxes
Because Partial Copy sandboxes cannot run Apex batch jobs at all
Because a sampled data subset can hide problems that only appear at full production data volume, which staging exists specifically to catch before production
Because Full sandboxes are cheaper to maintain than Partial Copy sandboxes
questions.explain: Staging's whole purpose is eliminating the 'worked in testing, broke in production' surprise -- a sampled dataset can mask exactly the kind of full-scale issue a Full sandbox would reveal.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce ships three major seasonal platform releases a year, and this course teaches that each one should be re-validated in ________ before it reaches production, because the platform itself can change underneath an org's own customizations.
questions.explain: Staging is where seasonal release testing happens -- refreshing staging, enabling the upcoming release preview, and re-running critical business processes against it before the release reaches production automatically.

questions.prompt: What does "change control" mean in a production context, per this course?
options: A once-a-year audit of every production user's license
Practices that keep every production change traceable, independently reviewed, and reversible
A Salesforce feature that automatically blocks all metadata changes
The process of renaming custom fields in production
A rule that only applies to changes made by outside contractors
An AppExchange package that encrypts production data at rest
questions.explain: Change control covers traceability of what changed and when, independent review before deployment, and the ability to reverse a change -- not a one-time audit or a single automated feature.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes a periodic audit, which is a one-time or scheduled check -- change control is an ongoing practice applied to every individual change, not a periodic review event.

questions.prompt: Put these four tiers of this course's default promotion path in the correct order, from where a change is first built to where it finally reaches real users.
items: Development -- a scratch org or Developer sandbox where the change is first built
Testing -- a Partial Copy sandbox where the change is validated against realistic data
Staging -- a Full sandbox used to rehearse the actual release
Production -- the org real users, customers, and integrations depend on
questions.explain: The promotion path runs Development to Testing to Staging to Production -- each stage resembling production more closely than the last, with nothing advancing past a stage it hasn't actually passed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Partial Copy sandbox has a minimum refresh interval of ________ days, meaning it cannot be refreshed more often than that, though it can always be refreshed less often.
questions.explain: Salesforce enforces a 5-day minimum refresh interval for Partial Copy sandboxes, between the 1-day minimum for Developer/Developer Pro and the 29-day minimum for Full.

questions.prompt: A developer has a half-finished Flow sitting in their personal Developer sandbox when a teammate refreshes it to pick up a recent production change. What happens to the half-finished Flow?
options: It is automatically merged into the refreshed copy
It is preserved indefinitely in a separate backup Salesforce maintains automatically
It is overwritten and lost, because a refresh replaces a sandbox's contents with a fresh copy from its source
Nothing happens to it -- refreshing a sandbox only affects its data, never its metadata
questions.explain: A refresh is destructive to anything not yet promoted out of the sandbox -- this is exactly why refresh timing needs to be planned and communicated, not done casually.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data risk in non-production environments, per this course.
options: A customer's real data is exactly as sensitive sitting in a sandbox as it is sitting in production
Sandboxes are sometimes treated with less rigor than production, which can make them the least protected place sensitive data exists
Only Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes can ever contain real production records
A wide-open sandbox access list combined with real sensitive data compounds the risk, rather than the two factors simply adding up independently
Data masking permanently removes the exposure risk of real data without requiring any access control at all
questions.explain: Data doesn't lose sensitivity by being copied into a sandbox, and looser sandbox rigor plus real data is a compounding risk. Partial Copy and Full (not Developer/Developer Pro) are the types that carry real data, and masking addresses the data side of risk -- it doesn't replace the separate need for access control.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between data masking and encryption, per this course?
options: Encrypted data is still the real data, mathematically recoverable with the right key; masked data has no key or permission level that recovers the original value
Encryption is one-way and irreversible, while masking can always be reversed with the right permission
Masking and encryption are the exact same technique with two different names
Masking only applies to numeric fields, while encryption only applies to text fields
questions.explain: Encryption always permits decryption for someone holding the key; masking is designed so that no one, including a sandbox's most privileged admin, can recover the real value -- a stronger guarantee for environments where no one should see the real data.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce Data Mask masking technique to what it does.
right: Replaces a field's contents entirely, for data a test scenario doesn't need present at all
Replaces a value with realistic-looking fake data drawn from the product's own libraries
Replaces a value with random characters when realism matters less than making the value unrecoverable
questions.explain: Realistic-value substitution keeps data looking real for UI walkthroughs; random-character replacement is cheaper when only populating the field matters; deletion removes the data entirely when a scenario doesn't need it present at all.

questions.prompt: Why does this course say sandbox access shouldn't automatically mirror whatever access a user already has in production?
options: Because sandbox access is always identical to production access by Salesforce design, with no exceptions possible
Because Salesforce technically prevents sandbox and production access from ever matching
Because only system administrators are ever granted any sandbox access

Because some users need broader sandbox access than production would suggest (a contractor building in a Developer sandbox), while others need narrower access (a sales rep with no reason to see a Full sandbox's real data)
questions.explain: Access needs can run in either direction relative to production -- scoping sandbox access deliberately, rather than copying production's list, is the least-privilege approach this course teaches.

questions.prompt: An org's environment diagram lists every environment and the promotion path, but leaves out whether each environment carries real, masked, or no data. What specific gap does this create?
options: None -- data posture is optional and rarely useful to document
It omits the diagram's data-posture layer, which is exactly what lets a security reviewer assess real risk without interviewing the architect directly
It means the diagram cannot show the promotion path at all
It means the diagram is only useful for enterprise orgs, not small teams
questions.explain: Data posture -- whether an environment carries real, masked, or no data -- is one of the five elements a real environment diagram needs, specifically because it communicates the risk surface covered in the data and masking lessons.

questions.prompt: A 15-person org's environment strategy deliberately skips a dedicated staging tier, using its Partial Copy testing sandbox as the final check before release instead. What risk does this design knowingly accept?
options: The risk that a bug which only shows up against full production data volume could reach production undetected
The risk that Salesforce will revoke the org's Salesforce license entirely
The risk that admins will permanently lose the ability to log into the org
There is no real risk -- skipping a staging tier has no downside at any org size
questions.explain: Without a Full-sandbox staging tier, a full-data-volume issue (like a batch job hitting governor limits only at real scale) could slip through -- a defensible bet for a small org without heavy batch processing, but a named, conscious trade-off, not an oversight.

questions.prompt: A large org has three teams with very different release cadences all sharing one testing and staging pipeline, causing frequent release delays. Why does this course say simply adding one more sandbox to the existing pipeline would not fix this?
options: Because Salesforce technically limits every org to a maximum of two sandboxes
Because sandboxes cannot be created for orgs in regulated industries
Because adding sandboxes becomes technically impossible once an org exceeds 100 users
Because it would just move the collision point rather than removing it, since the underlying issue is unrelated teams' work sharing a single serialized path to production
questions.explain: The root problem is structural -- different teams with different cadences forced through one shared, serialized pipeline -- which is why the fix is a multiple-pipeline strategy giving each team its own lane, not more capacity added to the same shared lane.

questions.prompt: Two independent pipelines each pass their own staging sign-off, but their changes conflict once both reach production in the same release. What does this course say is needed to catch this kind of cross-pipeline conflict?
options: Nothing can catch this -- cross-pipeline conflicts are an unavoidable cost of running multiple pipelines
Deleting one of the two pipelines so only one team can release at a time
A release train or coordinated deployment calendar, where each pipeline's changes are reconciled and sequenced before they all reach production together
Running each pipeline's staging sign-off twice instead of once
questions.explain: Each pipeline's own testing only validates its own changes in isolation -- a release train is the explicit coordination step that reconciles multiple pipelines' changes before they converge on production together.
